lessons.title: Estrus Detection and Synchronization
lessons.body: Estrus, or heat, is when a sow or gilt is ready to mate. Missing it wastes feed, time, and money. In Africa, where many farmers keep local breeds, heat signs can be subtle, so you must check twice dailyâearly morning and late eveningâfor 15 minutes each. Key signs: swollen, reddened vulva; mucus discharge; restlessness; grunting; and the standing reflex. To test the standing reflex, apply pressure on the sow's back near the tail. If she stands still and cocks her ears, she is in standing heatâthe best time to mate. Gilts (young females) cycle every 18â24 days, sows every 21 days. Heat lasts 2â3 days. For synchronization, you can use a boar to stimulate heat in groups of gilts. If you want to batch-farrow, use hormones like PG600 (400â800 IU) injected into gilts, but this requires a vet. Natural methods: mix new boars into the group, or move females to a new pen. In Africa, heat stress reduces conception, so provide shade and cool water. Record each heat date on a calendar or notebook. If a sow fails to show heat for 30 days, check for cysts or poor nutrition. Proper detection means you breed at the right time, saving money on feed and avoiding empty sows.

lessons.title: Mating Management and Artificial Insemination
lessons.body: Mating can be natural (boar to sow) or artificial insemination (AI). Natural mating: bring the sow to the boar's pen when she is in standing heat. A young boar can serve 2â3 times a week; a mature boar up to 6 times. Allow 15â20 minutes per service. If the boar is too heavy, use a mating crate. In Africa, many farmers use local boars, but they may be related, causing inbreeding. Rotate boars every 12â18 months. For AI, you need a trained technician, a semen catheter, and a dose of semen (80â100 ml with 3â5 billion sperm). AI is cheaper if you have many sows, as one boar's semen can serve 20â30 sows. Thaw frozen semen at 37Â°C for 15 seconds. Insert the catheter into the cervix, then slowly deposit semen over 5 minutes. Do not push air. After mating, keep the sow calm for 10 minutes. Best time to mate: 12â24 hours after standing heat begins. Mate twice, 12â24 hours apart, to increase litter size. Record the date and boar used. If using AI, order semen from a reputable lab. In hot climates, semen quality drops, so keep it cool. Proper mating management gives 90% conception and 10â12 piglets per litter.

lessons.title: Pregnancy Diagnosis and Farrowing Preparation
lessons.body: After mating, check for pregnancy. A sow that conceives will not show heat again in 21 days. That's the simplest test: watch for return to heat. If she doesn't, she's likely pregnant. For early detection, use an ultrasound scanner at 30 days. In Africa, where scanners are scarce, you can use a boar to test: if the sow refuses to stand for him, she's probably pregnant. Another sign: after 30 days, the vulva shrinks and becomes pale. By 60 days, the belly drops and teats enlarge. Prepare for farrowing (birth) 7 days before expected date. Clean and disinfect the farrowing pen. Use a broad-spectrum disinfectant like Virkon. Provide a farrowing crate or a corner with a rail to prevent crushing. Bed with dry straw or wood shavings. Reduce sow feed to 2 kg per day to prevent constipation. Wash the sow with warm water and mild soap, especially the udder and rear. Check for mastitis. Have on hand: iodine for navel, towels, gloves, and a heat lamp for piglets. In Africa, use a charcoal stove or lantern for warmth if electricity is unreliable. Keep the pen at 30â32Â°C for newborn piglets. Record the expected farrowing date (114 days after mating). If the sow shows no signs by day 118, call a vet. Good preparation saves piglets and keeps the sow healthy.

lessons.title: Farrowing Management and Assistance
lessons.body: Farrowing (birth) lasts 3â8 hours. Signs: restlessness, nesting, milk let-down, and a drop in body temperature. Be present or check every 30 minutes. Most piglets are born every 15â20 minutes. If a sow strains for more than 30 minutes without a piglet, assist. Wash hands, use gloves and lubricant. Gently insert a clean hand into the birth canal to check for a stuck piglet. Pull only with contractions. After each piglet: clear the mouth and nose with a towel, dry the body, tie the umbilical cord 2 cm from the belly with a clean thread, and cut with sterilized scissors. Dip the navel in iodine. Put the piglet under a heat lamp (30â32Â°C) or in a warm box with straw. Ensure each piglet suckles within 30 minutes to get colostrum. If a sow has more than 12 piglets, rotate them: let the smaller ones nurse first. In Africa, keep the pen quiet and dark. If the sow is aggressive, use a farrowing crate. After farrowing, give the sow warm water and 1 kg of feed. Check for retained placenta: if not passed within 4 hours, call a vet. Record number born alive, stillborn, and mummified. Good assistance reduces piglet deaths from crushing and starvation.

lessons.title: Lactation and Sow Care
lessons.body: A lactating sow produces 5â10 liters of milk per day. She needs high-energy feed: 2 kg for maintenance plus 0.5 kg per piglet. So a sow with 10 piglets gets 7 kg per day. Feed a lactation diet with 16â18% protein and plenty of clean waterâsows drink 20â30 liters daily. In Africa, use locally available feed like maize, soybean meal, and fish meal. Add minerals and vitamins. Keep the farrowing pen clean and dry. Check udders daily for mastitis: hot, hard, or painful quarters. If infected, strip the quarter and call a vet. Piglets need iron: inject 200 mg iron dextran at 3 days old. Also clip needle teeth at 3 days to prevent udder damage. Castrate males at 7â10 days. Provide a creep feed area for piglets from 10 days. Keep the sow cool: shade, fans, or wet the floor. Heat stress reduces milk. Wean piglets at 21â28 days. After weaning, reduce sow feed to 2 kg for 3 days to dry up milk. Then flush her with 3â4 kg for 7 days to bring her back into heat. Record weaning weight and sow condition. Good sow care means more piglets weaned and a shorter time to next litter.

lessons.title: Reproductive Efficiency Metrics
lessons.body: To know if your breeding program is working, track these numbers: conception rate, farrowing rate, litter size, and weaning rate. Conception rate = (number of sows pregnant / number mated) x 100. Aim for 85â90%. Farrowing rate = (number of sows farrowing / number mated) x 100. Aim for 80â85%. Litter size: born alive per litter. Good sows give 10â12. Weaning rate = (piglets weaned / piglets born alive) x 100. Aim for 90%. Also track weaning-to-service interval: days from weaning to next mating. Should be 5â7 days. If longer, check nutrition or health. Farrowing interval: days between litters. Target 145â150 days (114 days gestation + 21â28 days lactation + 5â7 days to rebreed). In Africa, record everything in a notebook or phone app. Calculate feed cost per piglet weaned. If a sow weans 10 piglets and eats 500 kg feed per year, and feed costs $0.30/kg, then feed cost per piglet = $150/10 = $15. If piglet sells for $30, profit is $15. Use these metrics to cull poor sows: any sow with less than 8 piglets born alive for two litters should be culled. Replace with gilts from high-performing litters. Good records help you make money, not just keep pigs.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Breeding and Reproduction in Pig Farming

In African pig production, reproductive efficiency determines whether a farm is profitable or merely surviving. A sow that weans fewer than 18 piglets per year consumes feed, labour, and housing without returning a profit. This practical reference distils the essential field procedures for estrus detection, mating and artificial insemination (AI), pregnancy diagnosis, farrowing management, lactation care, and the key metrics that tell you whether your breeding herd is working. It is written for farm managers and extension officers who need to act, not just understand.

Across sub-Saharan Africa, smallholder and medium-scale piggeries typically achieve 1.8â2.2 litters per sow per year, with pre-weaning mortality often exceeding 25%. Commercial benchmarks are 2.3â2.4 litters and under 12% mortality. Closing that gap is the single fastest route to higher margins, because every additional piglet weaned carries almost no extra feed cost beyond the sow's maintenance.

1. Estrus Detection and Synchronization

Estrus (heat) lasts 48â72 hours in gilts and 40â60 hours in sows, with ovulation occurring about two-thirds of the way through. The standing reflex â the sow freezing when pressure is applied to her back â is the single most reliable indicator. Detect it twice daily, morning and evening, using a boar in a nose-to-nose fence line. A teaser boar 10â15 metres away, moved closer, triggers the reflex within minutes.

Physical signs to score: swollen and reddened vulva, mucus discharge, restlessness, mounting pen-mates, reduced appetite, and erect ears. Record every observation. In African conditions where boars may be shared between farms, biosecurity during estrus checks is critical â use disposable boots and wash hands between units.

Synchronization is used to batch farrowings so that labour, farrowing crates, and piglet processing are concentrated. Common protocols:

  • PG600 (PMSG/hCG): for gilts and weaned sows that are not cycling. Administer 1 dose (5 mL) intramuscularly.
  • Altrenogest (Regumate): feed 15â20 mg/sow/day for 14â18 days, then withdraw; estrus follows in 4â6 days. Useful for gilts.
  • Prostaglandin (cloprostenol): for aborting or inducing farrowing, not for estrus sync in cycling sows.

In many African markets, PG600 and Regumate are expensive or unavailable. The cheapest synchronization tool is the boar: daily fence-line exposure of 15â20 minutes after weaning will bring 80â90% of sows into estrus within 7 days.

Table 1: Estrus detection signs and their reliability
SignReliabilityWhen to observe
Standing reflex (immobility)Very high (95%)Twice daily, with boar
Swollen, red vulvaModerate (70%)Early estrus
Mucus dischargeModerate (65%)Mid estrus
Restlessness / mountingLow (50%)Any stage
Reduced feed intakeLow (40%)Onset of estrus

Source: Adapted from FAO, Pig Sector Review and PIC Sow Management Guide (2020).

2. Mating Management and Artificial Insemination

Mating should be a planned event, not an accident. The golden rule is double service: serve the sow twice, 12â24 hours apart, timed to the standing reflex. For gilts, serve on the first day of standing and again 12 hours later; for sows, serve 12 and 24 hours after standing begins. This covers the ovulation window and lifts conception rate above 90%.

Natural mating ratios: one boar to 20â25 sows for hand mating, or 1:15 for pen mating. Boars must be rested â maximum two services per week for young boars, three for mature boars. Overworked boars produce poor-quality semen and lose libido.

Artificial insemination is increasingly viable in Africa where semen from superior genetics can be transported chilled (15â18Â°C) for up to 48 hours. The technique:

  1. Confirm standing reflex with boar contact.
  2. Clean the vulva with a disposable wipe; never use disinfectant inside.
  3. Insert the catheter at a 45Â° upward angle, then level out and rotate clockwise.
  4. Attach the semen bottle and allow gravity flow â do not squeeze.
  5. Maintain boar contact during insemination; 3â5 minutes per dose.
  6. Leave the sow undisturbed for 10 minutes after.
â  SAFETY WARNING â Boar Handling

Boars are the most dangerous animal on a pig farm. Never enter a boar pen alone, never turn your back, and always use a solid board or hurdle. In African heat, boars can become agitated rapidly. Keep a clear escape route. Children and untrained workers must never handle boars. For AI, always secure the boar behind a sturdy fence before working with the sow.

3. Pregnancy Diagnosis and Farrowing Preparation

Early pregnancy diagnosis saves money: a sow that is not pregnant should be re-served or culled immediately, not fed for 114 days. Methods available in Africa:

  • Ultrasound (day 21â28): most reliable; detects fluid and embryonic vesicles. Portable units now cost US$300â600.
  • Doppler / A-mode (day 30+): detects heartbeat or fluid; cheaper but less accurate early.
  • Not-in-estrus observation (day 18â24): free but only 70â80% accurate.
  • Vaginal biopsy / hormone tests: laboratory-based, rarely practical on-farm.

Once pregnancy is confirmed, manage the sow in three phases: early gestation (day 0â30) â 2.0â2.2 kg feed/day, avoid stress; mid gestation (day 31â90) â 2.2â2.5 kg/day, maintain body condition score 3; late gestation (day 91â114) â increase to 3.0â3.5 kg/day to support piglet growth and mammary development.

Farrowing preparation begins at day 110: wash and disinfect the crate, move the sow in, reduce feed to 2 kg/day, and provide clean bedding. Have on hand: iodine, clean towels, a heat lamp or heat box (32â35Â°C for piglets), and a farrowing record sheet.

Table 2: Reproductive efficiency benchmarks â African smallholder vs. commercial
MetricSmallholder typicalCommercial target
Litters per sow per year1.8â2.02.3â2.4
Piglets born alive per litter8â1011â13
Pre-weaning mortality20â30%<12%
Piglets weaned per sow per year14â1822â26
Weaning-to-service interval10â21 days4â7 days
Non-productive days (NPD)60â90<40

Source: Compiled from FAO Pig Sector Review (2012), ILRI smallholder pig value chain studies (Uganda/Kenya), and PIC Global Sow Productivity benchmarks (2021).

4. Farrowing Management and Assistance

Farrowing takes 3â8 hours; piglets are born at 15â20 minute intervals. Intervene only if the sow strains for more than 30 minutes without a piglet, or if a piglet is stuck. Wash hands, use lubricant, and gently assist â never pull with force. After each piglet: clear the mouth and nose, dry with a towel, dip the navel in iodine, and place under the heat lamp.

Watch for stillbirths (common after prolonged farrowing) and mummified piglets (indicate infection during gestation). Retained placentas beyond 4 hours require veterinary attention. Provide the sow with 2â3 litres of warm water with electrolytes immediately after farrowing.

5. Lactation and Sow Care

A lactating sow produces 5â8 litres of milk per day and must be fed 5â7 kg/day of a 16â18% protein diet, split into 2â3 meals. Water intake is 20â30 litres/day â a sow that cannot drink will not milk. Keep the farrowing pen at 18â20Â°C for the sow and 30â34Â°C for piglets; this temperature split is achieved with a heat lamp or creep box.

Monitor for mastitis-metritis-agalactia (MMA): hot, hard udder, fever, and piglets that are hungry and restless. Treat with veterinary antibiotics and anti-inflammatories. Body condition score the sow at weaning â target BCS 3 (ribs not visible but easily felt).

6. Reproductive Efficiency Metrics

Track these numbers monthly. They are the business dashboard of your breeding herd:

  • Farrowing rate: sows farrowed Ã· sows served Ã 100. Target >85%.
  • Litters per sow per year (LSY): 365 Ã· (gestation + lactation + weaning-to-service). Target 2.3+.
  • Piglets weaned per sow per year (PWSY): the ultimate profitability metric. Target 22â26.
  • Non-productive days (NPD): days a sow is neither pregnant nor lactating. Target <40.
  • Pre-weaning mortality: piglets dead before weaning Ã· born alive Ã 100. Target <12%.
  • Culling rate: 30â40% annually is normal; cull for repeat breeding, poor litter size, lameness, or age.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Check estrus twice daily with a boar; record standing reflex time.
  • â Double-serve every sow 12â24 hours apart; rest boars between services.
  • â Confirm pregnancy by ultrasound at day 21â28; re-serve or cull empty sows immediately.
  • â Move sow to a clean, disinfected farrowing crate at day 110.
  • â Attend farrowing; dry piglets, dip navels in iodine, provide heat at 32â35Â°C.
  • â Feed lactating sows 5â7 kg/day and ensure 20â30 L clean water daily.
  • â Record all reproductive events; calculate LSY, PWSY, and NPD monthly.
  • â Never handle a boar alone; always use a board and a clear escape route.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Good practices for the meat industry (pig section)
  • ILRI â Smallholder pig value chain publications (Uganda, Kenya, Vietnam)
  • The Pig Site â Practical reproduction and management articles
  • WOAH (OIE) â Terrestrial Animal Health Code (biosecurity and disease)
  • PIC â Sow management and reproduction guidelines (free registration)

quiz.q: What is the standing reflex in a sow?
options: A) She runs away from the boar
B) She stands still when pressure is applied to her back
C) She lies down and sleeps
quiz.explanation: The standing reflex indicates she is in standing heat and ready to mate.

quiz.q: How often should you check for estrus in sows?
options: D) Only when the boar is present
quiz.explanation: Checking twice daily (morning and evening) helps catch subtle heat signs.

quiz.q: What is the typical estrous cycle length for a sow?
quiz.explanation: Sows usually come into heat every 21 days if not pregnant.

quiz.q: Which hormone can be used to synchronize estrus in gilts?
quiz.explanation: PG600 contains pregnant mare serum gonadotropin and human chorionic gonadotropin to induce heat.

quiz.q: What is a natural method to stimulate estrus in a group of gilts?
options: B) Expose them to a boar
D) Keep them in the dark
quiz.explanation: The presence of a boar stimulates heat in gilts.

quiz.q: When is the best time to mate a sow after standing heat begins?
quiz.explanation: Ovulation occurs 12â24 hours after standing heat, so mating then maximizes conception.

quiz.q: How many times can a mature boar serve in a week?
quiz.explanation: A mature boar can safely serve up to 6 times per week without reduced fertility.

quiz.q: What is the recommended volume of semen for artificial insemination in pigs?
quiz.explanation: A standard AI dose is 80â100 ml containing 3â5 billion sperm.

quiz.q: Why should you rotate boars every 12â18 months?
quiz.explanation: Rotating boars reduces the risk of inbreeding and genetic defects.

quiz.q: What is the simplest way to check if a sow is pregnant after mating?
options: B) Watch for return to heat in 21 days
quiz.explanation: If the sow does not return to heat after 21 days, she is likely pregnant.

quiz.q: How many days after mating is the expected farrowing date?
quiz.explanation: The average gestation length for pigs is 114 days (3 months, 3 weeks, 3 days).

quiz.q: What should you do 7 days before farrowing?
options: B) Clean and disinfect the farrowing pen
C) Move the sow to a dirty pen
quiz.explanation: A clean pen reduces infections for the newborn piglets.

quiz.q: What temperature should the farrowing pen be for newborn piglets?
quiz.explanation: Newborn piglets cannot regulate body temperature well and need 30â32Â°C.

quiz.q: What is a sign that a sow is about to farrow?
quiz.explanation: Nesting behavior, restlessness, and milk let-down indicate impending farrowing.

quiz.q: What should you do if a sow strains for more than 30 minutes without delivering a piglet?
options: B) Assist with a clean, lubricated hand
quiz.explanation: Prolonged straining may indicate a stuck piglet, requiring manual assistance.

quiz.q: Why is it important for piglets to suckle within 30 minutes of birth?
options: A) To get colostrum for immunity
B) To keep the sow calm
C) To prevent them from fighting
quiz.explanation: Colostrum provides essential antibodies for the piglet's immune system.

quiz.q: What should you dip the piglet's navel in after cutting the cord?
quiz.explanation: Iodine disinfects the navel and prevents infection.

quiz.q: How much feed should a lactating sow receive per day if she has 10 piglets?
quiz.explanation: Feed = 2 kg maintenance + 0.5 kg per piglet = 2 + 5 = 7 kg.

quiz.q: What is a sign of mastitis in a sow?
quiz.explanation: Mastitis causes inflammation, making the udder hot, hard, and painful.

quiz.q: At what age should piglets be castrated?
quiz.explanation: Castration at 7â10 days is less stressful and heals quickly.

quiz.q: What is the recommended weaning age for piglets?
quiz.explanation: Weaning at 21â28 days balances piglet growth and sow rebreeding.

quiz.q: What should you do with a sow's feed after weaning?
options: B) Reduce to 2 kg for 3 days
quiz.explanation: Reducing feed helps dry up milk and prevents mastitis.

quiz.q: What is the target conception rate for a pig farm?
quiz.explanation: A well-managed farm should achieve 85â90% conception rate.

quiz.q: What is the target weaning-to-service interval?
quiz.explanation: Sows should return to heat and be mated within 5â7 days after weaning.

quiz.q: What is the target farrowing interval?
quiz.explanation: This includes 114 days gestation + 21â28 days lactation + 5â7 days to rebreed.

quiz.q: If a sow weans 10 piglets and eats 500 kg feed per year at $0.30/kg, what is the feed cost per piglet?
quiz.explanation: 500 kg x $0.30 = $150 total feed cost; $150 / 10 piglets = $15 per piglet.

quiz.q: When should you cull a sow?
options: A) After one litter with 12 piglets
B) After two litters with less than 8 piglets born alive
C) After three litters with 10 piglets
quiz.explanation: Poor reproductive performance over two litters justifies culling.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of flushing a sow after weaning?
options: B) To increase feed and stimulate heat
quiz.explanation: Flushing (increasing feed) boosts ovulation and litter size.

quiz.q: How much iron should be injected into piglets at 3 days old?
quiz.explanation: 200 mg iron dextran prevents anemia in piglets.

quiz.q: Why is heat stress a problem for breeding sows in Africa?
options: A) It reduces conception and milk production
B) It makes them eat more
quiz.explanation: High temperatures reduce conception rates and milk yield, so cooling is essential.
